family.label: Home & family
family.title: A fictional weekend planner
family.input: Three invented activities with prices, durations, and opening hours. Use no private family information.
checks: The total stays within a fictional $60 budget.
Activities do not overlap and fit within four hours.
An unavailable activity is flagged, not silently substituted.
family.transfer: One activity closes and your budget becomes $40. Revise the plan and explain what changed.

game.label: Games & play
game.title: A tabletop checkpoint game
game.input: Five invented checkpoints, scoring rules, and two fictional players. No real location tracking.
checks: A repeat check-in cannot award points twice.
A player can explain how the game ends.
An invalid checkpoint produces a clear exception.
game.transfer: A checkpoint becomes unavailable. Change the rules without creating an unbeatable game.

work.label: Work & operations
work.title: A synthetic reconciliation report
work.input: Two invented tables with record IDs and amounts. Include one mismatch, one missing record, and one duplicate. No employer data.
checks: Every mismatch and missing ID appears in the exceptions list.
A duplicate is flagged rather than counted twice.
Totals reconcile against a hand calculation.
work.transfer: Add a duplicate and a late correction. Explain how the result changes and which rows need human review.

product.label: My own product
product.title: A one-screen product prototype
product.input: One fictional user, one action, and three made-up records. Start on paper or with a local mock-up.
checks: The primary action works on a valid input.
An empty or invalid input gets a useful response.
The mock-up does not send information or pretend an external action succeeded.
product.transfer: A user provides missing information. Show how the interface recovers without guessing.

lessons.title: Give the assistant enough context
lessons.segment: Start with the introduction; then practice.
lessons.idea: An assistant works from the context and tools available in this session. Tell it what the result is for and what information it may use.
lessons.task: Write your desired outcome, permitted inputs, one unknown, and one action that needs your approval. Ask the assistant to reflect the brief before drafting.
lessons.question: You can open a company spreadsheet. Does that alone authorize uploading it to an AI service?
answers: No. Check the organization’s rules and the intended processing.
Yes, if a second model reviews it.
lessons.feedback: Access and authorization are separate. Use invented data for this exercise.
lessons.explain: What context does your assistant have, and what are you keeping outside this project?

lessons.title: Define the result
lessons.idea: Describe the decision or useful result, not just the document you want produced.
lessons.task: Make a one-page spec: outcome, intended user, inputs, constraints, assumptions, and a small first deliverable. Resolve one ambiguous decision.
lessons.question: Which is the stronger starting point?
answers: Find unmatched records so a reviewer knows what to investigate; include the source IDs.
lessons.feedback: The third answer names a purpose and evidence a reviewer can use.
lessons.explain: Which assumption did you resolve, and how did it change the spec?

lessons.title: Catch a mistake
lessons.idea: Decide how to check a result before building. A second opinion helps, but it does not replace evidence.
lessons.task: Predict the answer for a tiny input. Run one attempt. Compare it with your independent check, then deliberately introduce an error and see whether your check catches it.
lessons.question: Two models agree that a calculation is correct. What should you do next?
answers: Use a hand calculation or trusted executable check on the source inputs.
Ask the first model to sound more confident.
lessons.feedback: A source-based or executable check provides evidence beyond model agreement.
lessons.explain: What error did your check catch? What could the check still miss?

lessons.title: Make it repeatable
lessons.segment: 0:34–3:00 first; longer coding demos are optional.
lessons.idea: Keep the inputs, instructions, and checks needed to repeat the work outside one long chat.
lessons.task: Write a reusable instruction file with when to use it, required inputs, steps, checks, and stopping conditions. Start a fresh session with a changed fictional input.
lessons.question: What belongs in a shareable skill?
answers: Private account credentials so it works immediately.
The procedure and checks, with sample data and separate configuration.
All your chat history and employer files.
lessons.feedback: Share the procedure and examples. Each person configures their own data, tools, and permissions.
lessons.explain: What did the fresh session need that the old chat had been supplying implicitly?

lessons.title: Work with another person
lessons.segment: 11:07–12:35 · boundaries; read the corrections in RESOURCES.md.
lessons.idea: Make the proposed action easy to review before it affects another person.
lessons.task: Prepare a draft for a fictional reviewer. Include sources, unresolved questions, the exact proposed action, and the point where approval is needed. Keep this exercise unsent.
lessons.question: A draft is complete, but sending has not been authorized. What is its status?
answers: Sent, because the text is ready.
Approved, because the assistant likes it.
Draft, awaiting the appropriate review or authorization.
lessons.feedback: Describe the actual state. Preparing a draft is different from sending it.
lessons.explain: What is the reviewer approving, and how would you tell whether the authorized action really happened?

lessons.title: Repeat safely
lessons.segment: Optional reading; developers can also use the software-factory video.
lessons.idea: A recurring workflow needs to remember what happened, including uncertain outcomes.
lessons.task: Make a local queue with item IDs, draft/in-progress/confirmed/unknown states, and a result reference. Dry-run it twice; simulate a crash after an attempted action. No real messages or submissions.
lessons.question: An action times out after submission. What happens next?
answers: Mark it unknown and reconcile a receipt or remote state before retrying.
Mark it confirmed because it was probably submitted.
lessons.feedback: Uncertain outcomes require reconciliation. A blind retry can duplicate an action.
lessons.explain: How does your workflow avoid duplicates, and what makes it stop?
